newsitem.title: UK: S&P rates Russian Federation 2.0 bln mark eurobond.
newsitem.headline: S&P rates Russian Federation 2.0 bln mark eurobond.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Thursday it had assigned its BB minus long-term rating to the Russian Federation's 2.0 billion mark Eurobond maturing in 2004.
"The outlook on the rating is stable," S&P said in a statement.

"With output poised to begin growing this year, the current account likely will shift from a 1.0 percent of GDP surplus in 1996 to deficits medium term," the agency said. "However, the public external debt burden could fall further assuming the fiscal deficit can be contained."
"Russia's manageable external debt service, along with continued official external financial support, consequently should cushion its credit standing against most economic and political shocks."
S&P said key factors constraining Russia's foreign currency rating included
-- The government's short economic management track record and the political and administrative difficulties it faces raising tax revenues.

"To date, Russia's fiscal consolidation efforts have relied heavily on sequestering cash expenditures, a costly practice and one difficult to sustain in the face of public sector wage arrears, as well as unmet social spending needs," S&P said.
"A planned nation-wide strike by unpaid state workers on March 27 attests to the persistence of the wage arrears problem."
S&P said last year's federal government revenues, at 9.7 percent of GDP, were well below the 11.1 percent budgeted and the 12 percent outturn in 1995.

"The 1997 budget law targets revenue at 15.9 percent of GDP, still an unrealistic target. Revenue collections during the first quarter will likely fall below 10 percent of GDP, which according to the budget law will trigger sequestration of expenditures by mid-April," the agency said.
-- The ongoing challenge of leadership in a country with a still developing democratic culture and political institutions.

S&P said President Yeltsin's prolonged illness, now apparently at an end, created a serious power vacuum that undermined the authorities' efforts to deal effectively with tax evasion, corruption, and payment arrears.

"The president clearly intends the government reshuffle now underway to signal a renewed determination to tackle these issues. It remains to be seen, however, whether the new administration will have the political will necessary to resolutely pursue reforms."
-- A weak legal system, including lax enforcement that continues to foster widespread corruption, discourages foreign investment, and acts as a drag on overall economic activity.
S&P said key elements supporting the ratings included
-- The policymakers' strong commitment to disinflation.
The agency said the rate of increase in consumer prices fell sharply to 21.8 percent at end-1996 from 156.7 percent the previous year and should slow further to 17-19 percnet by the end of 1997.
-- Moderate general government debt, estimated at 47 percent of GDP at end-1996, in line with that of similarly-rated sovereigns.
-- A manageable external debt service profile.

"Russia's net public external debt burden remains high at around 120 percent of exports, but generous rescheduling terms on debt of the former Soviet Union mean that total debt service (including obligations of banks and non-resident holdings of rouble debt) amounts to just 22 percent of exports this year -- less than that of most sovereigns with double B category foreign currency ratings," S&P said.
"The rescheduling accords oblige the government to amortize relatively little foreign currency debt over the next five years."
-- Backing from the IMF.

S&P said while the Fund had delayed disbursing some monthly tranches since the third quarter of 1996, it remained committed to the $10.2 billion three-year Extended Facility Programme, helping support the Central Bank's modest gold and exchange reserves, equal to two months of imports in 1996.
